catalog_quote: Stress [/] Stress is phonemic, but is not significant for all words and is therefore not indicated for every word in the story. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Rosen 1977 (NUSA 5) is an image-only PDF; I rendered p.38 and read it visually. Under the heading 'Stress', symbol [/], the text reads exactly: "Stress is phonemic, but is not significant for all words and is therefore not indicated for every word in the story. In general stress tends to fall on the second syllable of a word." The supporting remark under Vowels [a-] ("The line above the vowel indicates that it is pharyngealized. Pharyngealized vowels are phonemically distinct from non-pharyngealized vowels. Sometimes the pharyngealization of vowel may be used to indicate stress, for example na- 'that' often only differs from na in that the former is more stressed than the latter.") i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Wangka dialect (Riung/Rembong-Riung) word stress generally falls on the second syllable of the word; since roots are overwhelmingly disyllabic this amounts to final-syllable stress in most words (the acute accents Rosen writes in the text, e.g. nange', ta.u', wali', pa.i', weto'n, diku', all sit on the second = last syllable). Rosen adds that stress is 'phonemic' (contrastive for some words) and marks it only sporadically.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is called 'phonemic, but not significant for all words', implying some lexical exceptions to the second-syllable tendency (none listed). Pharyngealized (per Schmidt: glottalized) vowels can also signal emphasis/stress on a word (na- vs na 'that').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in transcription notes to a narrative text recorded in Wangka village, Dec. 1975; hedged ('in general.. tends to'). Not an analysis of phrase-level prominence; Rosen 1983:53 separately uses 'stress' for emphatic prominence of a word.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Rosen 1977) describes the speech of Wangka village (Riung district, Ngada), which Rosen calls 'the Riung language'; Glottolog files Wangka under remb1250 'Rembong-Wangka' (Schmidt 2014 and Asplund 2020 treat Wangka as a dialect of Rembong-Riung/Rembong-Wangka). Glottolog also has a separate languoid riun1237 'Riung' [riu]; Rosen's data are specifically Wangka, so remb1250 is the right key, but the statement should be tagged 'Wangka dialect'. Rembong proper (Elar, East Manggarai; Verheijen's dictionaries) is a different dialect cluster of the same language and is not covered by the quote.

Also: pharyngealization of a vowel 'may be used to indicate stress' (na- 'that' vs na). Acute accents in the text (nange', ta.u', wali', zea', pa.i', weto'n, diku', aka'k) sit on the second = final syllable of disyllables.

sources.citation: Schmidt, Christopher K. 2014 [2013]. Morphosyntax of Wangka, a dialect of Rembong-Riung. PhD dissertation, Rice University. xx+299 pp. Chapter 3 'Phonology', pp. 93-121.
sources.note: The only modern full description of a Rembong-Riung variety based on >1 year of fieldwork; ch.3 (inventory, glottalisation, schwa, phonotactics) almost certainly states the stress pattern even though the TOC has no stress heading, and would supersede Rosen's 1977 two-sentence note. Open access in principle, but the live bitstream is behind an AWS-WAF browser challenge, the DSpace backend returned HTTP 500 on all handle lookups today, and the only Internet Archive copy is truncated to 1 MiB of 22.8 MB.
